Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette:
Liam Weber is a 29-year-old salesman who had been hiking with friends in a state park the summer before he came to treatment, when a fast-moving flash flood tore through the canyon trail. What he remembers clearly is the sound first—a sudden roar that didn’t fit the quiet of the afternoon—followed by the sight of water and debris surging around the bend too quickly for anyone to make sense of it. He was knocked off his feet, scraped against rock, and separated from the others. He recalls clawing at mud and brush, convinced he was about to be pulled under, but there are also stretches he cannot account for at all. When he tries to tell the story now, he gets to the moment of the water hitting him and then loses whole pieces of time. More disturbing to him, sometimes he does not see anything in his mind at all; instead he is suddenly flooded by the same raw terror from that day, as if his body remembers what his mind cannot fully picture.

In the weeks afterward, places began to take on a charge he could not explain away. A city greenbelt behind his apartment, the outdoor section of a garden store, even a client meeting at a golf course could make his chest tighten before he consciously knew why. Working in sales meant driving all over the region and meeting customers in office parks, model homes, and occasional outdoor commercial sites, and he found himself scanning routes in advance to avoid anything with wooded paths, embankments, or even the smell of wet soil. When he did end up somewhere that resembled the canyon—open sky, brush, uneven ground—he could feel the event without a coherent picture, then fragments would force their way in and remembering brought back the same helpless terror he felt in the flood. Those moments made him feel exposed in a way he hated, as though simply being in the wrong place could strip him of control. Each time a place set him off like that, the judgment came with it almost immediately: that he was damaged now, too easily undone, and that the world was the kind of place that could turn dangerous without warning. Each time that happened, the place itself seemed to tell him something bleak about who he had become: that he was now the kind of man who could be undone by a patch of brush or the smell of wet earth, and that the world could turn dangerous without warning.

That sense of exposure gradually changed what he believed about himself. Liam had thought of himself as capable, independent, and good under pressure, traits he relied on in his work. After the flood, he had come to believe he did not know who he was anymore. Once he had concluded that he was damaged and that no one could really keep him safe, ordinary features of the landscape started to snag his attention everywhere; a drainage ditch by a parking lot, a stand of trees near a client’s office, even darkening clouds felt newly charged because his mind was already treating the world as if danger were hiding in it. He was unsettled by how quickly a physical location could undo him, and he took that as proof that something essential in him had been damaged. Being in nature now felt less like a preference and more like a test he was bound to fail. He also found himself thinking that other people were unreliable in a fundamental way. His friends had been there that day, but in his mind the lasting lesson was that when disaster comes, no one can really keep you safe. That belief sharpened his sensitivity to places and situations where he might be vulnerable, so his world began to organize itself around reading environments for danger.

His nights became one of the clearest expressions of that shift. Because he felt he could not rely on anyone and could no longer trust his own old sense of steadiness, he slept lightly and woke abruptly to check locks, windows, and the weather on his phone. The more certain he became that he was no longer steady and that safety depended entirely on his own vigilance, the more his mind snapped back to the flood itself, as if replaying it were the only way to stay prepared for what might break through again. He told himself he was being sensible, but he was also on guard in a constant, exhausting way, listening for sounds that did not belong. During the day he startled into brief flashback states in which he felt as if the flood were happening again, especially when he was emotionally off balance or caught in a place that reminded him of the canyon. Each episode reinforced his conviction that he was no longer the person he used to be, and that life had lost whatever coherence or meaning it had before. After these episodes, the thought landed hard and familiarly: if a smell or a sound could pull him out of the present this completely, then something in him must be permanently altered.

The gaps in his memory troubled him almost as much as the fear itself. He returned to them repeatedly, trying to force a full account, as if certainty might restore some order. Instead, the missing pieces made him feel even less anchored, and the terror that came with recall left him convinced that his mind was no longer trustworthy. That in turn deepened his pull to monitor the world around him for anything resembling the original setting. If his own memory could ambush him without warning, then any trailhead, landscaped retention pond, or patch of woods near a client’s property seemed potentially dangerous. He had started declining lucrative appointments that involved outdoor venues, inventing scheduling conflicts rather than explain why he could not stand there calmly and make small talk.

By the time he sought help, Liam was functioning, but narrowly. His manager had commented on his reluctance to take certain accounts, and he had begun to wonder how long he could keep arranging his job around avoidance. What finally pushed him into treatment was waking one night already halfway out of bed, heart pounding, certain for a few seconds that water was coming into the apartment. He was frightened not only by the intensity of these episodes, but by what they seemed to say about his future—that he might remain watchful, cut off, and estranged from himself indefinitely. More than anything, he wanted to feel that a place could just be a place again, and that he could enter it without bracing for his whole world to collapse.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that triggers or reminders directly lead to Liam’s negative beliefs about himself, others, or the world within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show Liam’s negative appraisals causing intrusive memory or recall phenomena within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly convey that Liam’s negative beliefs increase his sensitivity to or generation of triggers/reminders within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that Liam’s trauma memory or recall directly produces negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
